title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). Crucially, two preregistered design choices—shared_initial_generation (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions) and reuse of the same deterministic validator as both the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer—produced a deterministic ceiling effect in this run that rendered the primary estimand uninformative for assessing generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics. The preregistered design (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) used gpt‑5‑mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime guard and scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes) and shared_initial_generation semantics. Confirmatory outcomes (archived artifacts) show complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). We present the preregistered methodology, the exact artifact‑grounded results, a diagnostic analysis explaining why the design choices produced a ceiling, and concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden future benchmarks so they expose generator×guard interactions.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into network configuration artifacts and staged change workflows (canaries, progressive rollout, rollback). Prior work demonstrates that LLMs can produce syntactically plausible configuration templates in controlled settings, while separate work on verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair loops and deterministic network verifiers shows that post‑generation checks can materially reduce syntactic and semantic errors in IaC and related domains. However, the operational safety question for agentic NetOps pipelines is end‑to‑end: how do generator variability, runtime verification, staged rollout semantics, repair, and rollback interact to affect safe‑deploy outcomes? We preregistered a confirmatory paired study (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) to measure whether integrating a deterministic runtime validator with an LLM generator increases safe‑deploy rates relative to an LLM‑only pipeline under a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1).

Research question. Under the benchmark semantics used here, does integrating a deterministic runtime validator with an LLM generator increase the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline) measured on N=400 preregistered paired tasks.

High‑level contribution and key finding. We provide (1) a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; (2) exact, archive‑verifiable confirmatory results showing universal acceptance of shared generator outputs by the deterministic validator (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0); and (3) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis demonstrating that the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics combined with reusing a single deterministic validator produced a deterministic ceiling that makes the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard interaction in this run. From the archived traces we derive concrete, implementable benchmark‑hardening recommendations to preserve statistical signal in future confirmatory runs.
sections.related_work: This study sits at the intersection of intent→configuration generation, verifier‑guided IaC workflows, deterministic network verification, and agentic/tool‑augmented LLM systems. Prior intent‑to‑configuration work demonstrates that LLMs can synthesize usable configuration templates in benchmarks and testbeds (intent‑based translation, PreConfig, GraphSynth), but those studies typically evaluate generation quality or template utility rather than end‑to‑end staged rollout safety. In IaC and provisioning contexts, verifier‑guided loops (for example, TerraFormer and related verifier‑guided fine‑tuning approaches) report correctness gains by integrating policy checks into generation/repair pipelines; these motivate analogous integrations for NetOps but do not demonstrate production‑scale closed‑loop runtime blocking with staged rollouts. Deterministic verifiers and reachability tools (header‑space style, Kubernetes reachability analyses) effectively detect configuration errors in emulated and offline settings, but tool scope and modeling assumptions differ across works. Agentic and tool‑augmented LLM architectures (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestrations) expand functionality for AIOps/RCA tasks but introduce failure modes—hallucination, misapplied tools, and miscalibrated confidence—that motivate runtime guardrails and staged deployments. Surveys and reviews note an evaluation gap: community‑standard, action‑aware benchmarks that combine generation, runtime blocking, staged rollouts, repair, rollback, and provenance are limited. Our experiment operationalizes a compact action‑aware staging benchmark under a strict preregistered design to directly probe verifier utility under those constraints and to surface practical design pitfalls.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. The study was preregistered as cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1. The primary confirmatory estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (two‑sided inference, α=0.05). The preregistered analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) implements a permutation‑based paired difference test and reports exact permutation p‑values; an exact McNemar two‑sided test was also produced as a corroborating statistic. Bootstrap percentile 95% confidence intervals (seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) were frozen for secondary outcomes.

Adapter semantics, shared generation, and model‑call accounting. Execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with declared generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer. Critically, the preregistration set shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false): each task provoked a single deterministic LLM generation that was shared identically with both the baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded episodes. This design intentionally isolates the validator’s acceptance decision on identical generator outputs rather than exposing independent generator variance between conditions. The mapping between planned episodes and model calls follows directly from this choice: planned episodes = 800 (two episodes per task) while actual model_calls_used = 400 because the same single generator call served both paired episodes. We clarify this mapping here to resolve potential confusion about model call accounting.

Episode flow, validator policy, and repair rules. For each task the adapter requested a shared initial candidate from gpt‑5‑mini, delivered the identical candidate to both episodes, and (in the guarded episode) routed the candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which applied full intent‑constraint validation. The preregistered repair policy permitted up to one repair attempt in the guarded episode; repair invocations, repair_applied flags, validation_before/after states, and final validity decisions were recorded in validator_trace entries. In this execution repair_applied = false across all episodes.

Task generation, difficulty labels, and deterministic replay. Tasks were created deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each task record includes structured difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, pattern, required_command_count, and level ∈ {medium, hard, very_hard}). The preregistration required deterministic three‑replay consistency checks for each agent+simulator pair; any pair failing deterministic replay or encountering simulator errors would be flagged and excluded from the primary analysis per the predefined missingness_plan. In this run all three‑replay checks passed and no exclusions were applied.

Confirmatory analysis procedures. The primary paired test used exact permutation on paired safe‑deploy booleans with α=0.05 and reports exact p‑values. An exact McNemar two‑sided test is reported for corroboration. Sensitivity analyses described in the preregistration (treating excluded pairs as failures, restricted permutations) were available; no exclusions occurred so those are not needed here. Secondary outcomes (bootstrap CI for median time‑to‑rollback, repair counts, affected‑services distribution) were preregistered and were computed where applicable; repair and rollback metrics are reported as observed.

Repair, rollback, and validator diagnostics. Across the 800 episodes repair_applied = false and no rollbacks were invoked; validator_trace entries show validation_after.final_state matched expected_final_state for accepted configurations. These traces explain universal acceptance: when the shared candidate satisfied the intent‑constraint checks implemented in deterministic_netops_validator_v5, both episodes necessarily recorded a safe‑deploy outcome.

Task difficulty signals. Each task record contains a difficulty level label. Representative sample entries among the first six archived tasks show a variety of difficulty patterns (for example: 1 medium, 2 hard, 3 very_hard in the representative sample). The full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 tasks are archived in the execution task manifest (execution/task_manifest.jsonl) for auditor aggregation; these per‑task labels were used for preregistered difficulty‑stratified exploratory diagnostics in the artifact set.

sections.discussion:
Why the primary estimand became uninformative. Two preregistered design choices together produced the observed deterministic ceiling. First, shared_initial_generation intentionally removed generator variance by delivering identical LLM outputs to baseline and guarded episodes. Second, the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). When the deterministic validator accepts the shared candidate, both conditions record identical safe‑deploy outcomes and the paired difference must be zero. This is a construct‑validity outcome of the frozen design, not a general null statement about verifier utility across diverse generator/validator pairings.

Consequences for power, inference, and interpretation. The preregistered power calculation assumed non‑ceiling baseline rates and within‑pair variability sufficient to detect an absolute difference ≈0.10 with N=400. The observed ceiling invalidates those assumptions and collapses inferential uncertainty: permutation and McNemar tests correctly report p = 1.0, but those statistics do not provide evidence about generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics because the design prevented the guard from having an opportunity to intervene. Therefore the null result must be interpreted as an artifact of the preregistered design choices rather than a general claim that runtime verification lacks operational value.

Benchmark‑hardening recommendations (artifact‑grounded). Using the archived validator_trace and execution accounting we recommend concrete, implementable steps for future confirmatory runs:

1) Independent per‑condition generation: set independent_condition_generation = true so each condition receives an independently sampled generator output; this restores generator variance and enables guards to act on differing candidates.

2) Distinct runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer: use independent verifier implementations or a held‑out scorer for post‑hoc analysis to avoid conflating acceptance and scoring and to permit true adjudication of disagreements.

3) Controlled adversarial seeding: preregister a controlled fraction of perturbation/adversarial seeds to guarantee a measurable baseline failure rate and preserve power for detection.

4) Difficulty‑stratified sampling: ensure the benchmark contains an adequate proportion of very_hard patterns to produce non‑negligible error rates and thus statistical signal for guard efficacy.

5) Instrumented repair/rollback metrics: enable and record repair attempts, repairs applied, and time‑to‑rollback as preregistered secondary outcomes so operational mitigation performance can be quantified.

These recommendations are grounded in the archived traces (which include repair_applied, validation_before/after, and difficulty metadata) and the execution accounting that revealed shared generation semantics and model call counts.

Threats to validity and generalizability. Model and scope: the run used a single declared generator (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator; results do not generalize across models, validator implementations, or production heterogeneity. Construct validity: the same deterministic validator serving both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer conflates acceptance and scoring. Environment realism: the benchmark is synthetic and the simulator/validator do not model production telemetry noise or adversarial operator behavior. Adversarial robustness and human‑in‑the‑loop efficacy were not exercised here and remain open questions for follow‑on preregistered work.

Operational implications. For NetOps practitioners, our artifact‑grounded diagnosis highlights two practical lessons: (i) experiment designs that remove generation variance can hide the potential benefits of runtime guards; and (ii) independent adjudication channels (distinct scorers or human reviewers) are important for measuring guard impact. Benchmarks intended to validate runtime safety mechanisms should preserve signal for guard interventions by incorporating independent generation, adversarial perturbations, or heterogeneous validators.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on an action‑aware staging benchmark. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). This deterministic ceiling effect resulted from frozen design and implementation homogeneity and renders the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop interactions in this run. We archive the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility and to support hardened follow‑on experiments (independent generation, adversarial seeding, heterogeneous validators) that exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors. The artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations supplied here offer concrete steps researchers can preregister to preserve statistical signal when evaluating runtime verifier utility in NetOps settings.

limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: the experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for future work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and can be aggregated by auditors; this manuscript reports representative sample counts to illustrate benchmark diversity but does not fabricate aggregated counts absent explicit artifact summarization in the manuscript body.
